title: The royal secret
hookLine: Krishna promises the royal secret, and it turns out to be a riddle about where the world lives
carry: all beings rest in God, like wind in the sky
tomorrow: The one who offers a leaf

cards: Two armies are still waiting, conches ready. In the chariot between them, Krishna has been teaching for eight chapters.

Now he leans in, the way a friend does when the room goes quiet, and says: I'm going to tell you the most secret thing. Because you don't find fault. Arjuna has argued and questioned, but never sneered.
And the secret he gives a student like that isn't a password or a hidden rite. It's a riddle about where the whole world lives.

teach.b: Verse one: to you, who doesn't find fault, I'll tell the most secret knowledge, together with its realization. Verse two gives it a grand name: raja-vidya, raja-guhya.
The king of knowledge, the king of secrets, the highest purifier.
Then three surprising words: it's known directly, by experience; it's in line with dharma; and it's easy to practice. The deepest secret in the Gita is called easy. Here it is.
Verse four: all this world is pervaded by me, in my unseen form.
All beings rest in me, but I don't rest in them. Verse five turns it over: and yet beings don't rest in me either. Behold my divine power.
It's a riddle, on purpose. Verse six gives a picture to hold it: as the great wind, moving everywhere, always rests in space, so all beings rest in me. The wind moves; space doesn't.
The wind is in space, but space isn't pushed around by it, or used up by it. So everything is in Krishna, and nothing contains or disturbs him.
Yesterday's cycle comes back too, all beings going into his nature and sent forth again. Those actions don't bind me, verse nine says; I sit as if unconcerned, unattached.
Verse ten: under my eye, nature brings forth the moving and the unmoving, and the world turns.
That's the royal secret, as the Gita tells it, and one of Hinduism's biggest teachings: God isn't only above the world; the whole world lives inside God.
You're already inside the one you're looking for, like wind inside the sky.
God isn't somewhere far to travel to, and you aren't the one holding the world up.

how: Chapter nine, the raja-vidya raja-guhya yoga, is one of the most loved chapters of the Gita; many Hindus read it for its teaching that all beings rest in God and that devotion is easy and open to all.

o: the king of secrets, the highest one
a secret only priests may hear

Krishna says he is contained in all beings

Krishna tells the secret because Arjuna doesn't find fault
verse 1: to you, who doesn't sneer or find fault.

games.q: Krishna needs a picture for how all beings can rest in him without touching him. which does he use?
games.why: wind in space, verse 6. the great wind moves everywhere and always rests in space, which isn't moved by it.

practice: Picture a wide, open sky with wind moving through it, some gusts strong, some gentle, and let your thoughts be the wind. Each time a thought gusts through, notice the space it moves in.
You don't need to stop the wind; the sky doesn't mind it, so just rest as the sky.

If you pray, close the way many Hindus do: fold your hands and offer the whole windy sky back to Krishna, or to God in the form you love, with one quiet Om. If you don't pray, just let the last breath out slowly, and rest.

wordCard.voice: Raja-guhya. The royal secret, the king of secrets. Gita nine: all beings rest in God, as wind rests in the sky.

orig.note: Sanskrit: raja-guhya, the royal secret; guhya, secret, from guh, to hide.

carryVoice: Your line: all beings rest in God, like wind in the sky. The wind moves, and the sky holds it without being moved. That's day one hundred eighty-nine.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 9.4–9.10 (all beings rest in me; wind in space)
